subject: Physics
title: Alternating Current
summary: In AC, voltage and current vary sinusoidally: v = V₀ sin ωt. Household supply is 220 V, 50 Hz — 220 V is the RMS value; the peak is about 311 V. The average over a full cycle is zero, so RMS values are used for heating.
In a resistor V and I are in phase. An inductor makes the current lag by 90° (X_L = ωL, opposition grows with frequency); a capacitor makes it lead by 90° (X_C = 1/ωC, blocks DC completely).
In a series LCR circuit the total opposition is the impedance Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²). When X_L = X_C, Z = R is minimum and current is maximum — resonance (ω₀ = 1/√LC). Radio tuning works on this.
Only the resistor consumes power: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ. In pure L or C the average power is zero (wattless current). Transformers change voltage so that power can be sent far with low loss.

formulas.name: Instantaneous AC
formulas.formula: v = V₀ sin ωt;   i = I₀ sin(ωt ± φ);   ω = 2πf
formulas.mistake: Don't confuse ω with f — 314 rad/s means 50 Hz.

formulas.name: RMS and average values
formulas.formula: V_rms = V₀/√2 ≈ 0.707V₀;   I_rms = I₀/√2;   half-cycle average = 2V₀/π ≈ 0.637V₀;   full-cycle average = 0
formulas.mistake: AC meters read RMS; the peak of 220 V supply is 311 V, not 220 V.

formulas.name: Inductive reactance
formulas.formula: X_L = ωL = 2πfL;   current lags V by 90°
formulas.mistake: For DC (f = 0), X_L = 0 — an inductor does not block DC.

formulas.name: Capacitive reactance
formulas.note: For DC, X_C = ∞ — a capacitor blocks DC completely.

formulas.name: Series LCR impedance
formulas.mistake: Voltages don't add directly: V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²); V_L and V_C can each exceed the supply voltage.

formulas.name: Phase angle
formulas.formula: tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R;   X_L > X_C: current lags (inductive);  X_L < X_C: current leads (capacitive)
formulas.mistake: φ is between voltage and CURRENT, not between two voltages.

formulas.name: Resonance
formulas.formula: X_L = X_C ⇒ ω₀ = 1/√(LC), f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC));   Z = R, current maximum, φ = 0
formulas.mistake: Resonant frequency does not depend on R; R only changes the height and sharpness of the peak.

formulas.name: Quality factor and bandwidth
formulas.formula: Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C);   bandwidth Δω = R/L = ω₀/Q
formulas.note: Higher Q = sharper peak = smaller R.

formulas.name: Power in AC
formulas.formula: P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos φ = I_rms² R;   power factor cos φ = R/Z
formulas.mistake: V_rms × I_rms is the apparent power, not the real power (cos φ is missing).

formulas.name: Wattless current
formulas.formula: power component: I_rms cos φ;   wattless component: I_rms sin φ
formulas.note: In pure L or C current flows but average power is zero.

formulas.name: LC oscillations
formulas.formula: ω = 1/√(LC);   energy moves between the electric field of C and the magnetic field of L;   q = q₀ cos ωt
formulas.note: With resistance, the oscillations die out (damped).

formulas.name: Transformer
formulas.formula: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s  (ideal);   efficiency η = P_out/P_in
formulas.note: A transformer works only on AC; on DC it would just heat up.

formulas.name: AC generator
formulas.formula: ε = NBAω sin ωt;   ε₀ = NBAω
formulas.note: emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B (flux zero, changing fastest).

examples.title: RMS value and frequency
examples.problem: v = 311 sin(314t) volt. RMS voltage and frequency?
examples.solution: V_rms = 311/√2 ≈ 220 V. f = 314/2π ≈ 50 Hz — this is household supply.

examples.title: Complete series LCR
examples.problem: R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω, X_C = 40 Ω, V_rms = 200 V. Find Z, current, power factor, power and phase.

examples.title: Resonance
examples.problem: L = 0.5 H, C = 8 μF, R = 10 Ω. Resonant ω, f and Q?

examples.title: Step-up transformer
examples.problem: N_p = 200, N_s = 4000, V_p = 220 V. Find V_s. If the secondary current is 0.5 A, what is the primary current (ideal)?

examples.title: Wattless current
examples.problem: I_rms = 5 A and the current lags the voltage by 60°. Wattless component and power factor?
examples.solution: Wattless = I sin φ = 5 × 0.866 = 4.33 A. Power factor = cos 60° = 0.5.

examples.title: Choke with a bulb
examples.problem: A 100 V, 50 W bulb must run on a 200 V, 50 Hz supply using a series inductor. Find L.
examples.solution: Bulb: I = 50/100 = 0.5 A, R = 100/0.5 = 200 Ω. Z = 200/0.5 = 400 Ω. X_L = √(400² − 200²) ≈ 346.4 Ω. L = X_L/(2π × 50) ≈ 1.1 H. (A series resistor would also waste 50 W; the choke wastes almost nothing.)

examples.problem: L = 10 mH, C = 1 μF. Oscillation frequency?

examples.title: Transformer efficiency
examples.problem: The transformer above is 90% efficient with output 4400 V × 0.5 A. Input power?
examples.solution: P_out = 2200 W. P_in = 2200/0.9 ≈ 2444 W. The remaining ~244 W is lost as heat (copper, eddy-current and hysteresis losses).

topics.title: Why RMS
topics.explain: The RMS value is the DC value that produces the same heat in a resistor. For a sine wave RMS = peak/√2. Meters show RMS; insulation and capacitor ratings must allow for the peak.

topics.title: Phasors
topics.explain: AC quantities are drawn as rotating arrows (phasors) turning at ω. In R, V and I are along the same line; in L, V leads I by 90°; in C, V lags I by 90°. In LCR, V_L and V_C are opposite, so they partly cancel.

topics.title: Reactance and impedance
topics.explain: Reactance (X_L, X_C) is measured in ohm but consumes no energy — it stores and returns it. Impedance Z is the total opposition (R and reactance added like vectors).

topics.title: Facts at resonance
topics.explain: At resonance V_L = V_C (they cancel), the circuit is purely resistive, current and power are maximum. Below f₀ the circuit is capacitive; above f₀ it is inductive. In radio and TV tuning, C is varied to bring f₀ to the station's frequency.

topics.title: Power in AC circuits
topics.explain: Average power = V_rms I_rms cos φ. Pure R: cos φ = 1. Pure L or C: cos φ = 0 (wattless). Low power factor in factories means larger current and larger line loss, so capacitors are added to improve the power factor.

topics.title: Transformer working and losses
topics.explain: AC in the primary sets up a changing flux in the core, which induces emf in the secondary (mutual induction). Losses: copper (I²R — use thick wire), eddy currents (laminated core), hysteresis (soft iron core), flux leakage. Power is transmitted at high voltage so that current and I²R loss are small.

topics.title: AC generator
topics.explain: A rotating coil has flux NBA cos ωt, so emf = NBAω sin ωt. Slip rings deliver AC. In India f = 50 Hz.

ratta: V_rms = V₀/√2;  220 V ⇒ peak 311 V;  half-cycle average 2V₀/π.
P = V_rms I_rms cos φ;  cos φ = R/Z.
Transformer losses: copper, eddy, hysteresis, leakage.
